outline.chapter_title: Introduction: The Problem with Tokenization and the BLT Paradigm
outline.description: This chapter motivates the Byte Latent Transformer by reviewing the role of tokenization in modern LLMs, its limitations, and the high-level goals of BLT: a tokenizer-free architecture that dynamically allocates compute based on data complexity.
subtopics: The role of tokenization in existing LLMs and its heuristic nature
Limitations of fixed-vocabulary tokenization: domain sensitivity, noise sensitivity, lack of orthographic knowledge, and multilingual inequity
Why directly training on bytes has been prohibitively expensive at scale
The core BLT idea: dynamic patching based on next-byte entropy
Key contributions of the paper: matching Llama 3 performance, inference efficiency, robustness, and a new scaling dimension
High-level architecture overview: two small local byte-level models and a large global latent transformer

outline.chapter_title: From Bytes to Patches: Patching Methods
outline.description: This chapter covers the concept of patching as a mechanism for grouping bytes into computational units. It introduces formal definitions, compares multiple patching strategies, and explains why dynamic entropy-based patching is preferred.
subtopics: Formal definition of a patching function and its relationship to computational cost
Strided patching every K bytes: simplicity and its downsides
Space patching: using whitespace-like bytes as natural boundaries
Entropy patching: using a small byte-level LM to identify high-entropy byte positions as patch boundaries
Global entropy threshold vs. approximate monotonicity constraint for boundary identification
Incremental patching: the formal property required for autoregressive generation
Comparison of patches (dynamic, no fixed vocabulary) vs. tokens (BPE, fixed vocabulary)
How BLT redefines the tradeoff between vocabulary size and compute

outline.description: This chapter provides a detailed walkthrough of the three-component BLT architecture: the Latent Global Transformer, the Local Encoder, and the Local Decoder, including cross-attention mechanisms and hash n-gram embeddings.
subtopics: Architecture overview: global autoregressive model plus local encoder and decoder
Latent Global Transformer: block-causal attention, role as the main computational engine
Local Encoder: lightweight transformer with cross-attention for pooling bytes into patch representations
Encoder hash n-gram embeddings: incorporating byte n-gram context via hash functions and embedding tables
Encoder multi-headed cross-attention: Perceiver-style attention with patch-specific masking and pooling initialization
Local Decoder: decoding global patch representations back into raw bytes
Decoder multi-headed cross-attention: reversed query/key-value roles compared to the encoder
Architectural details: SwiGLU, RoPE, RMSNorm, Flash Attention, and Flex Attention for dynamic masks

outline.description: This chapter describes the datasets, training configurations, entropy model setup, and evaluation metrics used to conduct controlled comparisons between BLT and tokenization-based baselines.
subtopics: Pre-training datasets: Llama 2 dataset and BLT-1T dataset
Entropy model: architecture, training, and role in entropy patching
Entropy threshold selection and context handling for structured content
Equalizing context length to ensure fair comparisons between patch and token models
FLOPs estimation methodology for BLT components (encoder, global transformer, decoder, cross-attention)
Bits-Per-Byte (BPB) as a tokenizer-independent alternative to perplexity
Transformer architecture hyperparameters shared with Llama 3
BLT-specific hyperparameters: model scales (400M to 8B), learning rates, hash sizes, and optimizer settings

outline.description: This chapter presents the core scaling results, demonstrating that BLT matches or exceeds BPE-based models in compute-optimal settings, downstream task evaluations, and fixed-inference-flop scaling regimes.
subtopics: Parameter-matched compute-optimal scaling: BLT vs. BPE Llama 3 on Llama 2 data
The role of architectural improvements (cross-attention, n-grams) and dynamic patching in matching BPE scaling
Effect of patch size on scaling: patch sizes of 6 and 8 bytes vs. Llama 2/3 token sizes
Downstream task evaluations: BLT-Entropy vs. BLT-Space vs. Llama 3 on reasoning, knowledge, and coding benchmarks
Inference-time entropy threshold adjustment for improved task performance
Patches scale better than tokens: simultaneously increasing model and patch size under a fixed inference budget
Fixed inference-flop scaling study: crossover points where BLT surpasses BPE models
Observations on how larger patch sizes benefit from larger model scales

outline.description: This chapter evaluates BLT's advantages in robustness to input noise, character-level understanding, phonological awareness, and low-resource machine translation, along with a method for initializing BLT from pre-trained token-based models.
subtopics: Noisy data evaluation: AntSpeak, Drop, RandomCase, Repeat, UpperCase strategies on HellaSwag
Grapheme-to-Phoneme (G2P) conversion assessment using Phonology Bench
CUTE benchmark: composition understanding, orthographic similarity, and character manipulation
BLT's near-perfect performance on spelling tasks vs. token-based model struggles
Low-resource machine translation on FLORES-101: advantages for long-tail byte sequences
Byte-ifying pretrained models: initializing BLT's global transformer from Llama 3.1 weights
Distillation results: reduced training flops with competitive or superior downstream performance
Analysis of remaining gaps and implications for future pre-trained model conversion

outline.description: This chapter presents ablation studies that justify key design choices in BLT, including entropy model hyperparameters, patching scheme comparisons, cross-attention placement, n-gram hash embedding sizes, and local model depth.
subtopics: Entropy model hyperparameters: effect of model size (1M–100M) and context window (64–512) on scaling
Patching scheme ablation: strided vs. space vs. BPE vs. entropy-based patching under controlled context length
Downstream task comparison of patching schemes
Cross-attention ablation: placement in encoder and decoder, query initialization strategies
Cross-attention benefits on Common-Crawl and with larger patch sizes
n-gram hash embedding vocabulary size ablation: 0 to 500K hashes and diminishing returns
Complementarity of hash embeddings and cross-attention across data domains
Local model layer allocation: lightweight encoder with heavier decoder

outline.description: This chapter surveys the evolution of character- and byte-level language models, from early RNNs to modern patching-based transformer architectures, situating BLT within this landscape.
subtopics: Character-level RNNs: early motivations for character modeling and advantages on morphologically rich languages
Character-level transformers: challenges of scaling and the gap from word-level models
Byte-level models without patching: ByT5, CANINE, CharFormer, and MambaByte
Patching-based approaches: Hourglass Transformer, dynamic patching with learned boundary predictors, and arithmetic coding compression
MegaByte: fixed static patching and concatenation, and its limitations at scale
SpaceByte: whitespace-based patching with a local encoder model
How BLT advances beyond prior patching-based and byte-level work

outline.description: This chapter discusses the acknowledged limitations of BLT, promising directions for future research, and a synthesis of the paper's contributions and implications for the field.
subtopics: Limitations: reliance on BPE-derived scaling laws for training budget allocation
Wall-clock efficiency gaps vs. theoretical FLOP comparisons due to library optimizations for token-based models
Future work: end-to-end learned patching and dedicated BLT scaling laws
Future work: fully leveraging byte-ified pre-trained token models
Summary of contributions: dynamic compute allocation, matching Llama 3 at scale, inference efficiency, robustness
The new scaling dimension: simultaneously growing model and patch size under fixed inference budgets
Broader implications for tokenizer-free LLM architectures
